sceneHappening: Visions, a thorn in the flesh, and the Lord's answer: "My grace is sufficient for you"
summary: Paul says boasting is necessary, though not profitable, so he will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord. He knows a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven, whether in the body or out of the body he does not know, God knows; and was caught up into paradise and heard inexpressible words which a man is not permitted to speak. On behalf of such a man he will boast, but about himself he will not boast, except in his weaknesses. If he decided to boast he would not be a fool, for he would be speaking the truth, but he refrains so that no one will think more of him than what is seen in him or heard from him. "And because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, that I should not be exalted excessively. Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me. He has said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.' Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me. Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ's sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong." Paul has been a fool; they forced him to it, since they should have commended him, for he is not at all inferior to the "super-apostles," though he is nothing. The signs of an apostle were performed among them with all patience, by signs, wonders, and mighty works. The only way they were treated worse than other churches is that he did not burden them: "forgive me this wrong." He is ready to come a third time and will not be a burden: "I seek not your possessions, but you." Children should not save up for their parents but parents for their children, and he will gladly spend and be spent for their souls. He asks whether Titus and the brother took advantage of them. Now, they probably think he is defending himself to them, but he speaks in Christ for their building up. He fears that when he comes he will find them not as he wishes, and that he will find quarrels, jealousy, anger, rivalries, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder, and that his God may humble him before them, and that he will mourn over many who have sinned before and not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality they have practiced.
whySettingMatters: Paul describes himself in the third person ("a man in Christ"), a way of showing reluctance to boast and perhaps of signaling that the experience is not what defines him. The "third heaven" and "paradise" reflect Jewish ideas of layers of heaven; paradise here means God's presence, as in Luke 23:43. The date "fourteen years ago" would place the vision around AD 41 to 42, if the letter was written about AD 55 to 56, but the setting is not given. What "the thorn in the flesh" was has been debated since the early church: suggestions include an illness (eye trouble, malaria, epilepsy), a recurring temptation, or a human opponent. Paul calls it "a messenger of Satan," which would suit a person (the verb "to torment" is the word for striking a blow), but the text does not say, and the lack of detail is part of its use: any person can find themselves in it. Notice that Paul does not say God removed it; he says the Lord answered and gave something different. The signs and wonders of an apostle (12:12) echo Romans 15:19. Paul's treatment of money (12:13-18) shows again that some in Corinth had suspected him of using the collection for himself, which is why Titus and the brothers were chosen as named, trusted agents.

people.note: Describes a vision and a thorn, and learns that weakness is where power rests.
Went to Corinth with a brother; Paul asks if he took advantage.
Outside teachers whom Paul says he is not inferior to.
Paul's children, whom he is about to visit a third time.
The Lord who answered Paul's prayer: "My grace is sufficient for you."

questions: Paul keeps the vision to himself for fourteen years and talks about it reluctantly. What does that say about how he views spiritual experiences?
He asked three times for the thorn to be taken away, and the answer was "my grace is sufficient." How do we hold a "no" and a promise together?
What does it mean that "power is made perfect in weakness"?
Paul says parents should save for their children, not the other way around. How does he apply that to his own relationship with the Corinthians?
